Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR *When `glyphs` is omitted, MapLibre GL JS (v5.11 + ) automatically falls back to **local‑font rendering**. The engine draws the text with the browser’s normal CSS font‑family resolution (system fonts or any web‑font you have loaded with `@font-face`). If the requested font isn’t available locally, the browser falls back to its generic “sans‑serif” (or whatever the OS decides), which is why you see a “generic” font on the map.* It’s **not a bug** – it’s the intended behaviour introduced in PR #4564. Below is a step‑by‑step of what’s happening, why you’re seeing the generic font, and what you can do to get the exact font you want. --- ## 1. What the spec says vs. what the engine does | Situation | Style spec (pre‑v5.11) | MapLibre GL JS ≥ 5.11 | |-----------|-----------------------|----------------------| | `glyphs` **present** and reachable | Must fetch glyph‑PBFs for every `text-font`/range. If a request fails, the whole tile is considered missing → the layer disappears. | Same, but if a particular range fails, the engine **gracefully falls back** to local rendering for that range only (log message, no tile error). | | `glyphs` **omitted** | Invalid according to the original style spec – most implementations would error out. | Treated as “local‑fonts mode”. Every `text-font` entry is resolved exactly like a CSS `font-family` list. No glyph‑PBFs are ever requested. | So, with **no `glyphs` field** you are now in the *local‑fonts mode*. --- ## 2. What “local‑fonts mode” actually does 1. **Collect the `text-font` array** for each symbol layer. Example: ```json { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": "{name}", "text-font": ["My Custom Font Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"] } } ``` 2. **Ask the browser to resolve the first name** (`"My Custom Font Regular"`). - If a **web‑font** with that exact `font-family` name has been loaded via `@font-face` (or is a built‑in system font), the browser uses it. - If the name is **unknown**, the browser falls back to the next entry in the list (`"Noto Sans Regular"`). - If none of the names resolve, the browser finally falls back to its generic default (`sans-serif`, `system-ui`, etc.). 3. **Render the text with TinySDF** (a tiny signed‑distance‑field generator that runs in the main thread). - This is **pixel‑perfect** for the chosen font at any zoom, just like a pre‑generated glyph PBF would be. - It **does not** use any glyph‑PBF server, so there is no network traffic for text. 4. **CJK special case** – `localIdeographFontFamily` (default `'sans-serif'`) overrides any `text-font` for Chinese/Japanese/Korean characters. The engine always draws those characters locally, regardless of the `text-font` list, because serving CJK glyph ranges would be extremely heavy. (You can change the on‑device font via the map option, see below.) --- ## 3. Why you see a *generic* font | Reason | What to check / fix | |--------|---------------------| | **The font isn’t loaded** (no `@font-face` or not installed on the OS). | Add a proper `@font-face` rule **before** you create the map, and make sure the `font-family` name matches exactly the string used in `text-font`. | | **Name mismatch** (e.g., you wrote `"MyCustomFont"` but the `@font-face` uses `"My Custom Font"`). | Font names are case‑sensitive and must match *exactly* (including spaces). | | **CJK characters** – you’re looking at Chinese/Japanese/Korean labels. | Those ignore `text-font`. Use `localIdeographFontFamily` to pick a nicer on‑device CJK font, or set it to `false` if you *must* use served glyphs (slow and heavy). | | **Browser fallback chain** – the OS doesn’t have the requested font, and you didn’t provide a web‑font. | Install the font on the machine (for testing) or ship it as a web‑font. | | **Font weight/style not available** – you asked for `"My Custom Font Bold"` but only the regular weight exists. | Include the specific weight in your `@font-face` or add a fallback weight in the `text-font` list. | If none of the above apply, open the browser console. You’ll see a log like: ``` [maplibre-gl] Unable to load glyph range 0-255.pbf for font "My Custom Font". Rendering codepoint U+4E2D locally instead. ``` That message tells you the engine tried to fetch a glyph PBF (because a `glyphs` URL is present *somewhere* in the style hierarchy) and fell back to local rendering. In pure “no glyphs” mode you’ll see instead: ``` [maplibre-gl] No glyphs URL defined – using local fonts. ``` --- ## 4. How to get the exact font you want ### Option A – Keep the “local‑fonts” approach (recommended for most web maps) 1. **Load the font as a web‑font** (or be sure it’s installed on the client OS). ```html ``` 2. **Make the `text-font` entry match the `font-family` name exactly**. ```json "text-font": ["My Custom Font Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"] ``` 3. **(Optional) Pre‑load the font** so the map doesn’t flash with the fallback before the font is ready: ```js document.fonts.load('12px "My Custom Font Regular"').then(() => { // now create the map const map = new maplibregl.Map({ /* … */ }); }); ``` That’s all – no `glyphs` field, no server, no PBF generation. ### Option B – Switch back to the classic glyph‑PBF workflow If you need **pixel‑perfect cross‑platform parity** (e.g., you ship the same style to MapLibre Native, where the local‑font fallback isn’t implemented yet), you should: 1. **Add a `glyphs` URL** that points at a glyph server (MapLibre’s demo server, OpenMapTiles, or your own). ```json "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf" ``` 2. **Make sure the server hosts the exact font‑stack folders** (`My Custom Font Regular/0-255.pbf`, etc.). - For standard fonts (Noto, Open Sans, Roboto) you can copy the pre‑built tree from the **openmaptiles/fonts** repo. - For a brand‑new font, generate the PBFs with **Font Maker** or **fontnik**, then serve them. 3. **Keep `text-font` unchanged** – the engine will now request the PBFs instead of using the browser’s font resolution. > **Note:** In this mode CJK characters will still be rendered locally unless you set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` (slow) or provide CJK glyph PBFs (huge). ### Option C – Hybrid: serve glyphs for non‑CJK, keep local for CJK ```js const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: 'style.json', // Keep the default localIdeographFontFamily (or set a nicer on‑device CJK font) // CJK will be rendered locally, everything else via glyph PBFs. }); ``` --- ## 5. Quick checklist for “my font isn’t showing” | ✅ | Action | |---|--------| | **1** | Verify that `glyphs` is **absent** (or deliberately omitted). | | **2** | Confirm the font you want is **available locally** (system install or `@font-face`). | | **3** | Ensure the `font-family` name in `@font-face` **exactly matches** the string in `text-font`. | | **4** | If you use a web‑font, preload it (`document.fonts.load`) **before** creating the map. | | **5** | Check the console for any “Unable to load glyph range …” messages – they indicate the engine fell back because it *couldn’t* find a glyph PBF. | | **6** | For CJK text, remember `text-font` is ignored; set `localIdeographFontFamily` if you want a specific on‑device CJK font. | | **7** | If you need identical rendering on MapLibre Native, add a proper `glyphs` URL (or use the Native `font-faces` property). | --- ## 6. Example – Full working snippet (local‑font mode) ```html MapLibre – Local Font Example
``` *Result:* All labels appear in **My Custom Font Regular** (or fall back to Noto Sans if the font fails to load). No network requests for `*.pbf` files. --- ## 7. Bottom line - **No `glyphs` → local‑font fallback** (expected, not a bug). - The generic font you see is simply the browser’s fallback because the requested font isn’t available locally. - **Fix it** by loading the desired font as a web‑font (or installing it on the client) and making sure the name matches the `text-font` entry. - If you need *exact* cross‑platform rendering (e.g., for a native app) or want to avoid reliance on the client’s font stack, add a proper `glyphs` URL (or use Native’s `font-faces`). Feel free to ask if you need help wiring a glyph server, generating PBFs for a custom font, or configuring the RTL plugin for Arabic/Hebrew scripts!

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step‑by‑step recipe** for getting **offline, local‑font label rendering** with **MapLibre Native on Android**. It assumes you are using **MapLibre‑Android ≥ 11.13.0** (the first version that ships the `font‑faces` property) and that you want **zero network traffic for text** – i.e. no `glyphs` URL, no external glyph‑PBF server. --- ## 1. The big picture | Platform | How MapLibre finds a glyph | What you must provide | |----------|---------------------------|-----------------------| | **GL JS** (≥ 5.11) | If `glyphs` is missing **or** a glyph‑PBF fails, it falls back to **TinySDF** and renders the text with any web / system font you have loaded. | Nothing extra (just optional `@font‑face` rules). | | **MapLibre Native (Android / iOS)** | **Never** falls back to TinySDF. It only knows two ways to get a glyph:
1️⃣ a `glyphs` URL that returns SDF‑PBFs, **or**
2️⃣ a **`font‑faces`** block that maps a `text‑font` name to one or more **local TTF/OTF files** (plus the Unicode ranges they cover). | You must add a `font‑faces` block to the style and ship the referenced font files with the app. | So for an offline Android app you **cannot rely on the GL JS “omit‑glyphs → local‑font” trick** – you have to use the **`font‑faces`** mechanism. --- ## 2. Bundle the font files 1. **Pick the fonts you need** *For a world‑wide map the safest choice is the **Noto** family because it ships a separate font for each script (Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Devanagari, CJK‑SC, CJK‑TC, …).* 2. **Copy the `.ttf` / `.otf` files into your Android project** ```text app/ src/ main/ assets/ fonts/ NotoSans-Regular.ttf NotoSans-Bold.ttf NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf // optional – huge, see note below ``` *The `assets/` folder is automatically packaged into the APK and can be read with `AssetManager`.* 3. **(Optional) Reduce size** – If you only need a subset of Unicode, you can create a *subset* of the Noto CJK font with tools like **pyftsubset** (part of `fonttools`). This can shrink a 30 MB CJK file to a few MB while still covering the codepoints you actually use. --- ## 3. Create the `font-faces` block The `font-faces` property lives **inside the style JSON**, at the same level as `sources`, `layers`, `glyphs`, etc. ```json { "version": 8, "name": "Offline‑Noto‑Style", "sources": { … }, "layers": [ … ], // ------------------------------------------------- // 1️⃣ Omit the `glyphs` field – we are not using a server // ------------------------------------------------- // "glyphs": "https://example.com/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", // ------------------------------------------------- // 2️⃣ Add a `font-faces` block that points to the bundled fonts // ------------------------------------------------- "font-faces": [ { "font-family": "Noto Sans Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans Bold", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSans-Bold.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0000-00FF, U+0100-024F, U+0250-02AF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0600-06FF, U+0750-077F, U+08A0-08FF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": "U+0900-097F, U+0980-09FF" }, { "font-family": "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular", "src": "asset://fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": "U+4E00-9FFF, U+3400-4DBF, U+20000-2A6DF" } ] } ``` ### Key points | Field | What it means | |------|----------------| | `font-family` | Must **exactly match** the string you use in `text-font` arrays in your layers. | | `src` | `asset://` tells the native SDK to load the file from the APK’s assets. You can also use `file://` for an external path (e.g. a downloaded font). | | `unicode-range` | A **comma‑separated list** of Unicode ranges that this file covers. MapLibre will only load the file when a label contains a code‑point inside one of those ranges. Keep the ranges as tight as possible – it reduces memory usage and speeds up look‑ups. | | **Order matters** – If two `font-faces` entries overlap, the first one wins. | > **Why not a single “Noto Sans” file?** > The Noto family is split into many sub‑fonts precisely to keep each file small and to avoid loading huge CJK tables when you only need Latin. The `unicode-range` field lets you keep the same logical family name (`Noto Sans`) while pointing to different physical files. --- ## 4. Reference the fonts in your style layers ```json { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], // Fallback list – try Latin first, then Arabic, then Devanagari, then CJK "text-font": [ "Noto Sans Regular", "Noto Sans Arabic Regular", "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular", "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular" ], "text-size": 12 }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ``` *MapLibre will walk the `text-font` list, pick the first entry whose `font-faces` block covers **all** code‑points in the label, and render with that font.* If a label contains a mix of scripts (e.g. “Москва Москва” – Cyrillic + Latin), the first font that covers **every** character wins; otherwise it falls back to the next entry. --- ## 5. Initialise the map – nothing special beyond a normal `MapView` ```kotlin val mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView) mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap -> // Load the offline style you just created (it can be a raw JSON string, // a file in assets, or a URL on the device) mapboxMap.loadStyleUri("asset://style/offline-noto-style.json") } ``` *No `glyphs` URL, no network request for text.* All glyphs are read from the bundled TTF/OTF files via the `font-faces` block. --- ## 6. Special considerations ### 6.1 CJK (Chinese/Japanese/Korean) * **Why we still need a local font file** – Native does **not** have the GL JS “localIdeographFontFamily” shortcut. If you omit a `font-faces` entry for CJK, the SDK will try to fetch glyph‑PBFs (which you said you don’t want). * **Performance tip** – CJK ranges are huge (tens of thousands of code‑points). If you bundle the full Noto CJK font (≈30 MB) you’ll increase APK size, but you’ll avoid any network traffic. *If you only need a limited set of characters (e.g. city names in a single country), use `pyftsubset` to create a **tiny** CJK subset and list only that range in `unicode-range`.* ### 6.2 Scripts that need shaping (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Khmer, etc.) *MapLibre Native **does not** perform complex text shaping.* It will draw each Unicode code‑point as a separate glyph. This works for Arabic/Hebrew **only if you also load the RTL text plugin** (the same plugin used by GL JS). The plugin reorders the characters and adds the necessary mirroring. ```kotlin // Must be called **before** any map is created MapLibre.getInstance(this).setRTLTextPlugin( "file:///android_asset/maplibre-gl-rtl-text.js", // you can ship the file in assets null, true // true = load synchronously (simpler for offline) ) ``` *Devanagari, Khmer, Burmese, etc.* – these scripts need **ligature shaping** that MapLibre currently cannot do. Even with the correct font file you will see missing conjuncts. The only workaround today is to **pre‑render the label as an image** (e.g. via a server‑side tile service) or accept the degraded appearance. ### 6.3 Font‑family naming conventions * The name you put in `font-family` **must be exactly** the string you use in `text-font`. * Do **not** include the weight/italic suffix in the name unless you have created a separate entry for it (as shown for “Noto Sans Bold”). * If you want to use the same TTF for both regular and bold, you can list it twice with different `font-family` values and rely on the `text-font` list to pick the right one. ### 6.4 Updating the style at runtime If you later download a new font (e.g. a user‑specific brand font) you can: 1. Save the `.ttf` into the app’s private storage (`context.filesDir`). 2. Add a new entry to the **in‑memory** style JSON: ```kotlin val newFace = JSONObject() .put("font-family", "My Brand Font") .put("src", "file://${context.filesDir}/MyBrand.ttf") .put("unicode-range", "U+0000-00FF") styleJson.getJSONArray("font-faces").put(newFace) mapboxMap.setStyle(Style.Builder().fromJson(styleJson.toString())) ``` The SDK will pick it up immediately; no app restart needed. ### 6.5 Testing that you are truly offline 1. Turn off Wi‑Fi / mobile data. 2. Open the map. 3. Verify **no network requests** appear in Logcat for `*.pbf` or `*.json` under the domain you would have used for a glyph server. 4. All labels should still appear, using the fonts you bundled. If a label disappears, check the `unicode-range` of the matching `font-faces` entry – the code‑point is probably outside the range you declared. --- ## 7. Full minimal example (project‑level) ``` app/ └─ src/ └─ main/ ├─ assets/ │ ├─ style/ │ │ └─ offline-noto-style.json ← style with font-faces │ ├─ fonts/ │ │ ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf │ │ ├─ NotoSans-Bold.ttf │ │ ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf │ │ ├─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf │ │ └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf │ └─ maplibre-gl-rtl-text.js ← copy from CDN

I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?

Description: negative — out-of-scope question about hillshade/terrain layers
prompt: How do I add a hillshade layer from a raster-dem source to my MapLibre GL JS style?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a complete, step‑by‑step recipe for adding a **hillshade** layer that is driven by a **raster‑DEM** source to a MapLibre GL JS map. It works with any DEM that you can serve as a raster tile set (e.g. GeoTIFF‑based tiles, Cloud‑Optimized GeoTIFFs, or a simple XYZ/WMTS endpoint). --- ## 1. Prepare the DEM tiles | Option | How to get it | Typical URL template | |--------|---------------|----------------------| | **Open‑source DEM tiles** (e.g. OpenTopoMap, USGS, Copernicus) | Use an existing public service or host your own with `tileserver-gl`, `tegola`, `martin`, `geoserver`, etc. | `https://mytileserver.org/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | | **Cloud‑Optimized GeoTIFF (COG)** | Store a COG in S3, Azure Blob, or any HTTP‑accessible bucket and use a raster‑DEM source that points to the COG URL. | `https://mybucket.s3.amazonaws.com/elevation.tif` | | **Self‑hosted XYZ tiles** | Generate tiles with `gdal2tiles.py`, `maptiler`, `tippecanoe` (for raster) or `rio‑tiler`. | `https://myhost.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.png` | **Important:** The DEM must be **single‑band** (elevation values) and **pixel‑values must be in metres** (or you must tell MapLibre the correct `encoding`). Most public DEM services already meet this requirement. --- ## 2. Add the raster‑DEM source to the style You can either: * **Inject the source via JavaScript** (good for dynamic styles) * **Add it directly to a JSON style file** (good for static styles) ### 2.1 JavaScript (dynamic) ```js // Assuming `map` is an instance of maplibregl.Map that is already loaded map.addSource('my-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', // For XYZ/WMTS tiles: // url: 'https://mytileserver.org/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png', // For a single COG: // url: 'https://mybucket.s3.amazonaws.com/elevation.tif', // Common options: tileSize: 256, // 256 or 512 – must match your tiles maxzoom: 14, // highest zoom you have tiles for // Optional: if your DEM is encoded as 16‑bit unsigned integers (most are) // you can tell MapLibre to treat it as such: // encoding: 'mapbox' // default, works for most Mapbox‑style DEMs }); ``` ### 2.2 JSON style (static) ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "my-dem": { "type": "raster-dem", "url": "https://mytileserver.org/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", "tileSize": 256, "maxzoom": 14 } }, "layers": [ /* … later we’ll add the hillshade layer … */ ] } ``` > **CORS tip:** If the DEM tiles are on a different origin, make sure the server sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or the specific origin of your page). Otherwise the raster‑DEM source will fail to load and the hillshade layer will stay invisible. --- ## 3. Add the hillshade layer MapLibre provides a dedicated **`hillshade`** layer type that consumes a `raster-dem` source. The layer has a handful of paint properties that let you control illumination, exaggeration, and color. ### 3.1 Minimal example (JavaScript) ```js map.addLayer({ id: 'hillshade', type: 'hillshade', source: 'my-dem', // name of the source added above layout: {}, // hillshade layers have no layout properties paint: { // Optional – defaults are shown for reference 'hillshade-illumination-direction': 335, // degrees clockwise from north 'hillshade-illumination-anchor': 'viewport', // or 'map' 'hillshade-exaggeration': 0.5, // 0 = flat, >1 = more pronounced 'hillshade-shadow-color': 'rgba(0,0,0,0.5)', 'hillshade-highlight-color': 'rgba(255,255,255,0.5)', 'hillshade-accent-color': 'rgba(255,255,255,0.2)' } }); ``` ### 3.2 Full example (JSON style) ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "my-dem": { "type": "raster-dem", "url": "https://mytileserver.org/dem/{z}/{x}/{y}.png", "tileSize": 256, "maxzoom": 14 } }, "layers": [ { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", "source": "my-dem", "paint": { "hillshade-illumination-direction": 315, "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "viewport", "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.7, "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(0,0,0,0.6)", "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,255,255,0.5)", "hillshade-accent-color": "rgba(255,255,255,0.2)" } } ] } ``` > **Why a separate `hillshade` layer?** > The `hillshade` type does the heavy lifting of converting elevation values into a shaded relief image on the GPU. It is far more efficient than pre‑rendering hillshades as raster tiles. --- ## 4. Fine‑tuning the visual appearance | Paint property | What it does | Typical values | |----------------|--------------|----------------| | `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Sun azimuth (degrees clockwise from north). | 0‑360 (e.g., 315 for a north‑west sun) | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Whether the sun direction stays fixed to the viewport (`viewport`) or rotates with the map (`map`). | `"viewport"` (default) or `"map"` | | `hillshade-exaggeration` | Vertical exaggeration of the terrain. | `0` (flat) → `2` (very dramatic). 0.5‑1.0 is common. | | `hillshade-shadow-color` | Color of the shadowed side. | `rgba(0,0,0,0.5)` (default) | | `hillshade-highlight-color` | Color of the illuminated side. | `rgba(255,255,255,0.5)` | | `hillshade-accent-color` | Color of the “mid‑tone” accent (helps bring out subtle relief). | `rgba(255,255,255,0.2)` | **Tip:** Play with `hillshade-exaggeration` together with `hillshade-illumination-direction` to get the exact look you want. Small changes are often enough to make the terrain pop without looking unrealistic. --- ## 5. Ordering the layer Hillshade is usually placed **below** any label or symbol layers but **above** the base raster or vector background. In a typical style you might insert it like this: ```js // Insert hillshade just above the background layer map.addLayer({ id: 'hillshade', type: 'hillshade', source: 'my-dem', // … }, 'water'); // insert before the layer named "water" ``` If you have a `background` layer, you can also use `'background'` as the insertion point. --- ## 6. Full minimal working example (HTML + JS) ```html MapLibre Hillshade Demo
``` Open the file in a browser (or serve it via a local web server) and you should see a shaded‑relief map over the OpenStreetMap base. --- ## 7. Common pitfalls & troubleshooting | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **Hillshade layer is invisible** | DEM source fails to load (404, CORS, wrong `tileSize`) | Open the network tab, verify tile URLs, add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, ensure `tileSize` matches the source (256 vs 512). | | **Only flat gray terrain** | `hillshade-exaggeration` set to `0` or DEM values are all zero | Check the DEM data (use a viewer like QGIS). Increase `hillshade-exaggeration`. | | **Banding / pixelated shading** | Using low‑resolution DEM (e.g., maxzoom 8) at high zoom levels | Provide higher‑resolution DEM tiles or limit the map’s max zoom. | | **Craters or “holes” where tiles don’t line up** | Tiles from different sources have mismatched extents or projection | Ensure all DEM tiles use the same Web Mercator (`EPSG:3857`) tiling scheme. | | **Performance drops on mobile** | Very high `hillshade-exaggeration` + high‑resolution DEM | Reduce `maxzoom` of the DEM source or lower `hillshade-exaggeration`. | | **Hillshade disappears after style reload** | Layer added before the source is ready (e.g., using `addLayer` before `style.load`) | Wait for the `style.load` event or add the layer in the `styledata`/`sourcedata` callbacks. | ```js map.on('style.load', () => { // safe to add source + hillshade now }); ``` --- ## 8. Optional enhancements | Feature | How to add | |---------|------------| | **Terrain 3‑D extrusion** (e.g., building extrusions) | Add a `terrain` property to the map: `map.setTerrain({ source: 'my-dem', exaggeration: 1.5 });` | | **Dynamic sun direction** (e.g., animate sunrise) | Update `hillshade-illumination-direction` via `setPaintProperty` in an animation loop. | | **Blend hillshade with a vector style** | Keep your vector style as the base, add the DEM source, then add the hillshade layer *below* the vector layers you want to keep on top. | | **Offline usage** | Store the DEM tiles (or a single COG) in the browser’s Cache API or IndexedDB and point the source URL to a `blob:` URL. | | **Custom color ramps** | Use `hillshade-shadow-color`, `hillshade-highlight-color`, and `hillshade-accent-color` to mimic a specific cartographic style (e.g., “relief shading” vs “terrain shading”). | --- ## 9. Recap checklist 1. **Serve a raster‑DEM** (XYZ tiles or a COG) with proper CORS. 2. **Add a `raster-dem` source** (`type: 'raster-dem'`). 3. **Add a `hillshade` layer** that references that source. 4. **Tune paint properties** (`illumination-direction`, `exaggeration`, colors). 5. **Insert the layer in the correct order** (below labels, above base raster). 6. **Test & debug** with the browser dev tools (network, console).
